name: The Sacraments/Ordinances: Baptism and Communion

objectives.text: Identify water as the sign used in baptism and bread and the cup as the signs used in the Lord's Supper
Retell the account of Jesus sharing bread and the cup with his disciples on the night he was betrayed
Recall that Jesus commanded his church to baptize and to eat the Lord's Supper in remembrance of him
Retell New Testament accounts of people being baptized in the early church
Describe the words, actions, and signs used when a church administers baptism and the Lord's Supper, including baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Explain that baptism signifies washing from sin and marks a person as belonging to God and his people
Explain that the Lord's Supper remembers and proclaims Christ's death until he comes again
State the Westminster Shorter Catechism definition of a sacrament and explain each of its parts in their own words
Distinguish between a sign and the thing it signifies using the water of baptism and the bread and cup of the Supper as examples
Explain why the Reformed tradition recognizes only two sacraments instituted by Christ in the New Testament
Explain how Scripture connects baptism to union with Christ in his death and resurrection
Describe whom the Reformed tradition teaches should come to the Lord's Supper and explain the biblical call to self-examination before coming
Explain the Reformed teaching that sacraments become effective means of grace through the blessing of Christ and the work of the Spirit rather than through power in the elements or the minister
Explain how the Lord's Supper expresses believers' communion with Christ and their unity with one another as one body
Compare the terms sacrament and ordinance and analyze what each emphasizes about baptism and the Lord's Supper
Analyze how Scripture connects circumcision as an Old Testament covenant sign to baptism
Interpret Jesus' words "This is my body" in their context by comparing them with other figurative statements in Scripture
Explain how the Passover meal anticipates and shapes the meaning of the Lord's Supper
Explain why the Reformed tradition administers baptism once while the Lord's Supper is repeated and how it relates baptism's efficacy to the time of administration
Examine the biblical evidence used in debates over the mode of baptism and state the Westminster Confession's position on sprinkling, pouring, and immersion
Construct a biblical argument for infant baptism as the Reformed tradition holds it and summarize the credobaptist case accurately and fairly
Explain what the Westminster Larger Catechism means by improving one's baptism and describe practices it recommends
Evaluate transubstantiation, the Lutheran view, the memorial view, and the Reformed view of Christ's spiritual presence in the Lord's Supper against Scripture
Evaluate the Reformed critique of the Mass as a sacrifice in light of the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ
Analyze Paul's warning against eating and drinking in an unworthy manner within the context of Corinthian divisions and explain its bearing on the church's practice of guarding the Table
Create a teaching presentation that explains how baptism and the Lord's Supper function as visible words that sign and seal the gospel promise

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (signs of each sacrament, Christ's command, meaning of baptism and the Supper, sign versus thing signified, who should come, sacrament versus ordinance, This is my body, circumcision and Passover connections, infant baptism debate, views of presence, 1 Corinthians 11 warning, visible words). Dropped the observation objective because seeing a service is not an assessable competency and replaced it with describing the words and actions used. Added missing competencies: the institution narrative, Acts baptism accounts, the catechism definition of a sacrament, why only two sacraments, union with Christ in baptism, efficacy through the Spirit, communion and unity in the Supper, once-for-all baptism versus a repeated Supper, mode of baptism, improving one's baptism, and the critique of the Mass. Anchored each to verse-level Scripture and specific Westminster and Heidelberg articles and left general worship elements to sibling sub-topics.
